intro: A college player and a big-league player both sign papers that decide where they may play. For the college player, the papers are scholarship and eligibility forms. For the professional, they are contracts. For more than a century, the people who wrote those papers were mostly college leaders and team owners, not the players.

This unit follows two long arguments. The first asks whether a college athlete is a student, a worker or both. It runs from a railroad-sponsored rowing race in 1852 to the NCAA's founding in 1906, a Supreme Court ruling in 2021 and a 2025 settlement that let schools pay athletes. The second asks who owns a professional career. It runs from baseball's reserve clause of 1879 to Curt Flood's lawsuit and the free agency players won in 1976.

Chicago and Illinois appear often: the 1895 Chicago meeting that began the Big Ten, the first basketball championship final in Evanston in 1939, Rube Foster's league and the 2014 union vote at Northwestern. By the end, you will be able to name the laws, cases and agreements that moved power, and argue which ones mattered most.
bigQuestion: Who should decide where an athlete plays and what an athlete is paid: the school, the owner, a court, a union or the athlete?

timeline.t: Harvard and Yale row the first U.S. intercollegiate race
National League owners agree to reserve five players per club
Colleges form the IAAUS, renamed the NCAA in 1910
Rube Foster founds the Negro National League in Kansas City
Supreme Court rules in Federal Baseball Club v. National League
Supreme Court rules against Curt Flood in Flood v. Kuhn
Arbitrator Peter Seitz frees Andy Messersmith and Dave McNally
NCAA v. Board of Regents ends the NCAA football TV plan
NFL agreement brings veteran free agency and a salary cap
NCAA v. Alston decided; college athletes may earn NIL money
House settlement lets schools share revenue with athletes

allowed under the rules to play or compete
an athlete who competes without being paid

law that protects competition and forbids agreements that fix prices or limit markets
name, image and likeness; a person's identity used to promote or sell something

test.q: Who paid the travel costs for the first intercollegiate race in 1852?
test.why: The Boston, Concord and Montreal Railroad paid, hoping to sell trips to the lake.

test.q: Why was the IAAUS founded in 1906?
choices: to answer deaths and injuries in college football
test.why: After the deaths of 1905, colleges met and formed a national rule-making body.

test.q: Where was the 1895 meeting that began the Big Ten held?
test.why: Purdue's president called leaders to Chicago in January 1895.

test.q: What did the 1984 case NCAA v. Board of Regents decide?
choices: Players may be paid for NIL.
The NCAA's football TV plan broke antitrust law.
test.why: The Court ruled 7 to 2 that the plan restrained competition.

test.q: According to Walter Byers, what was the term student-athlete meant to do?
choices: counter the idea that players were employees
replace the word amateur at the Olympics
test.why: Byers wrote in 1995 that the term answered workers' compensation claims.

test.q: What did NCAA v. Alston (2021) decide?
choices: The NCAA must pay every athlete a salary.
The NCAA could not cap education-related benefits.
College athletes must join a union.
test.why: The Court ruled 9 to 0 that caps on education-related benefits broke antitrust law.

test.q: Which founder of a Black baseball league owned the Chicago American Giants?
test.why: Rube Foster founded the Negro National League in 1920.

test.q: What did John Montgomery Ward argue in 1887?
choices: The reserve rule protected players' wages.
The NFL should hold a draft.
The reserve rule treated players like property.
test.why: His article asked whether the ballplayer had become a chattel.

test.q: Why did Justice Holmes say baseball was exempt from antitrust law in 1922?
choices: He said baseball exhibitions were not interstate commerce.
He said Congress had passed a special law.
He said the Federal League had broken its contracts.
test.why: Holmes treated the games as local business, making travel only incidental.

test.q: How did Flood v. Kuhn (1972) treat baseball's exemption?
choices: It called the exemption an anomaly but left it for Congress to change.
It extended the exemption to football.
It said the reserve clause was an arbitration matter only.
test.why: Justice Blackmun kept the 1922 precedent and said Congress should act.

test.q: Which decision first freed players from the reserve clause's endless renewals?
test.why: Seitz ruled the clause bound a player for one renewal year only.

test.q: What did Marvin Miller win for baseball players in 1968?
choices: the first collective bargaining agreement in pro sport
test.why: The 1968 agreement raised the minimum salary to 10,000 dollars.

test.q: What did NFL players accept in 1993 along with free agency?
test.why: The 1993 agreement paired veteran free agency with a team spending limit.

test.q: Which is a college case, not a professional one?
choices: Federal Baseball Club v. National League
test.why: Ed O'Bannon sued the NCAA over the use of college players' likenesses.

test.q: What did Spencer Haywood's 1971 case challenge?
choices: the NBA's rule barring players until four years after high school
test.why: Haywood argued the NBA's four-year rule was an illegal agreement among teams.

write.prompt: Pick one: Is a college athlete today more like a student or a worker? Or: Which single event did most to give pro athletes control of their careers? Argue from at least three dated cases, laws or agreements in this unit. Name each one and its year, say what it decided, and explain how it moved power.
tips: Name each case, law or agreement with its year, such as NCAA v. Alston (2021).
Say who made each decision: a court, a legislature, an arbitrator or a bargaining table.
Give the strongest point for the other side, then answer it.
Use the unit's terms, such as reserve clause, free agent and antitrust law.
Keep facts and your opinion apart: say what happened first, then what you think it means.
